newsitem.title: USA: FBI's "most wanted" list still full of fugitives.
newsitem.headline: FBI's "most wanted" list still full of fugitives.

text.p: The suicide of an accused multiple killer wanted for murdering fashion designer Gianni Versace took one fugitive off the FBI's 10 most-wanted list, but still leaves a number of career criminals and alleged terrorists.

After suspected Versace murderer Andrew Cunanan killed himself on a houseboat in Miami Beach on Wednesday, the FBI put the words "Found Dead" across his photograph on its Web site on the Internet that displays its most-wanted fugitives.

FBI officials said Cunanan's death underscored the success of the programme, which was created in 1950 as a publicity device by the legendary FBI Director J. Edgar Hoover to get the public's help in tracking down dangerous criminals.
Cunanan, the focus of one of the biggest manhunts in U.S. history, became the 422nd person captured or located out of 449 fugitives who have been placed on the list, they said.
"We've had a lot of cases solved over the years," FBI Deputy Director William Esposito said. "And almost half of all the fugitives who were caught ... were caught because citizens called in tips."

There now are eight fugitives on the list due to Cunanan's suicide and last month's capture in Pakistan of Mir Aimal Kansi, who was brought back to the United States to stand trial for killing two CIA workers in a 1993 shooting spree outside the spy agency's headquarters.
Those on the list range from little-known career criminals such as cop killers and murderers to fugitives with alleged links to extremist groups.
Still wanted are two Libyans who have been charged in the United States and Britain with the 1988 bombing of Pan Am Flight 103 over Lockerbie, Scotland that killed 270 people.
Abdel Basset Ali Megrahi and Lamen Khalifa Fhimah, two accused Libyan intelligence officers, were placed on the FBI list in 1995.
The fugitive on the list the longest, since 1981, has been Donald Webb, a burglar who specialised in jewelry stores. He disappeared after the shooting death of a Pennsylvania police officer in 1980.

Among the others are Victor Gerena, charged with a $7 million armed robbery in 1983 of a Connecticut security firm, and Arthur Washington, who associated with militant black groups and allegedly killed a New Jersey trooper in 1989.

"In the 1970s, the top 10 list included many fugitives with with organised crime ties or links to terrorist groups. This emphasis continues today, along with serial murders and drug-related crimes," one FBI official said.
To be placed on the list, FBI officials said fugitives first must be considered a particularly dangerous menance to society or have a lengthy record of serious crimes.
Next, the officials said the FBI must believe that nationwide publicity will help apprehend the fugitive.

The officials said publicity for the progream has changed over the years, starting out first in newspapers, then in radio and television shows and now in cyberspace with the list on its Web site -- www.fbi.gov.
